new_statements.rule_in_words: Hmong Njua is a tone language with seven lexical tones (pp. 10-11). The only stress the thesis describes is sentence-level emphatic stress: 'sentence stress' can be placed on any word in a sentence to emphasize it (p. 134); emphasis is otherwise carried by intonation raising and by vowel lengthening / tone raising (pp. 33, 133). No word-level stress rule is stated (the language is essentially monosyllabic and the thesis is a syntactic description; the author himself says 'more study of the Hmong Njua phonology should be done', Abstract p. i).
new_statements.exceptions: none; stress is described only as free, emphatic, sentence-level placement ('on any words in a sentence')
new_statements.identity_note: Kunyot 1984 describes Hmong Njua (Green Hmong, Blue Meo; self-name 'Mong Njua'/'Mong Leng') as spoken in Ban Khek Noi, Lomsak District, Phetchabun Province, Thailand, from fieldwork Nov 1983-Mar 1984 with three young helpers; the author warns (p. 2) that the variety in that village may have assimilated toward White Hmong (Hmong Daw), which is the majority there, and that the two dialects are 'quite similar in both phonology and grammar' (p. 7). Tone transcription follows Lyman 1970. Mortensen 2004 (not obtained) is a phonology of the same variety, Mong Leng.

(2) Deciding source: a 2021 741-pp PhD grammar (Glottolog's top 'grammar' entry for hmon1264) whose phonology chapters include per-syllable duration/intensity/F0 measurements; it explicitly says there is no meaningful lexical stress contrast and describes an optional, pragmatically conditioned final-syllable (iambic-like) word prominence plus seven lexical tones — exactly what the record codes (classification tonal, the primary-stress rule final prominence, the secondary-stress rule initial intensification, =os exception). No JIPA Illustration or dedicated stress study of Green Mong was found; the instrumental literature (Andruski & Ratliff 2000 JIPA; Andruski 2006) concerns tone/phonation. Mortensen 200

tone.quote: This paper presents the acoustic portion of a cross-gender study on acoustic and perceptual correlates of the breathy tone in Green Mong. Three male and three female native speakers of Green Mong residing in the Detroit area were asked to produce a series of target words containing the breathy tone and comparison tones in sentence context. Target words were minimal sets in which only tone varied. ... Four acoustic correlates of tone (fundamental frequency or F0, F0 contour, duration, and breathiness) were measured in each target word.
